reasons: Scott: The most actionable ladder: it pre-clears 96.8% of heat-pump requests, applies a derate band for hourly data, gives a correct break-even, and proposes a 90-day shadow pilot scored against engineers' study outcomes. The vendor-style pricing per meter is out of place for an internal tool.

Bruce: 'Thermostats for peak, batteries for upgrades' is backed by a computed break-even, a short-peak confidence band, 96.8% heat-pump pre-clearance and a 90-day shadow pilot, which is the most deployable storage framework of the set.

Andrew: Very clear and operational, with pre-clearing of requests and a confidence band for short peaks, but its money slide can only be a break-even and the pay-per-meter framing reads like a vendor pitch.
Mike: A clean per-meter callable screen that answers one question per home and includes a 15-minute derate band, but the business case is still a break-even on an unsourced upgrade cost.

Brian: This is the strongest of the ladder variants: a per-home callable function, a derate band for the peaks hourly data hides, correct break-even arithmetic ($6k to $14k), and a shadow pilot scored against engineers' verdicts. The analytics are still thin.

Rogerio: The only ladder that derates for hidden 15-minute peaks and proposes a shadow pilot scored against real engineering-study outcomes, which is how my team would actually adopt a meter-based screen.

Enrique: It is the best-executed ladder: the break-even arithmetic ($6k-14k per home) checks out against the facts, a derate band covers short peaks, and a 90-day shadow pilot on real load-add requests makes it deployable.

Claudia: The clearest ladder: it screens real load-add requests, pre-clears the 96.8% of heat-pump adds, derives a $6k-14k break-even from facts.json, and carries a short-peak derate band, though the per-meter vendor pitch reads oddly for a utility audience.

Maureen: One plain question per home, a traced $6k-14k break-even, and a 90-day shadow pilot against engineering studies make this the most usable and teachable BESS framework, though the pay-per-meter pitch is odd for an internal utility.
blockers: No avoided service-upgrade or engineering-study cost anywhere in facts.json or citations.yaml. This is a soft blocker: the whole business case collapses to a break-even unless a sourced number is found, and the 40% Solution and Business Value criterion asks for quantified impact.

How to read the 3 kVA rule is a judgment call that cannot be tested. The challenge says a 200 A service 'should not exceed approximately 3 kVA of additional incremental load without further evaluation'. bess.py reads that as new peak <= old peak + 3 kW. If the judges (Reliability, Load Research) read it as connected load, every 7.2 kW L2 charger needs a study regardless, and the ladder below 'needs study' has no meaning. This must be stated on the slide.

The 2-unit rung passing 100% is true by construction (7.68 kW continuous > 7.2 kW charger, energy covers 2 h), not an empirical result. Presented as evidence it will cost credibility with technical judges.

The managed-charging definition swings the result. In a read-only sample, 7.2 kW in the best 2-hour window passes about 28% of homes, while 3.6 kW over 4 overnight hours passes about 88%. A realistic power-limited managed rung could clear most EV requests without a battery, which weakens the 'batteries for upgrades' headline to about 12% of homes.

No ground truth: no engineering-study outcomes, transformer or feeder map, or panel data, so the verdict's accuracy cannot be validated in this event. It can only be proposed as a 90-day shadow pilot.
Hourly averages hide 15-minute peaks, so any derate is an assumption and not a measurement.
The 'homes without EV' pool includes unlisted chargers (EV L2 held-out recall is only 30.7%), and 10,072 of 35,725 customers are missing, so counts apply to 25,653 homes only.
No tariffs: the $359/yr bill savings and $100/kW-yr capacity value inside the break-even are both assumptions.
table.fallback: If time runs short, cut back to three things: the per-home rung CSV for EV L2 and heat pump with three rungs (as-is, managed charging at one stated definition, program battery), the ladder figure with the sub-hourly derate band, and a break-even slide showing the avoided-upgrade cost per home the battery needs to justify itself (about $6k to $14k, with every input labeled ASSUMED), with no sourced upgrade cost. That version also drops the confidence band to a single derate assumption and states plainly that the 2-unit rung clears by construction. The pilot becomes one bullet: score 'needs study' verdicts against engineer outcomes on incoming NYSEG/RG&E load letters. The analysis is about 4 to 5 h on top of bess.py and can be finished even if the upgrade-cost search fails. It still scores on the rubric's electrification enablement, BESS prioritization and actionability lines.

reasons: Scott: Dating when each charger first appears gives a meter-measured EV adoption rate, a load research insight nobody else offers, but its managed-charging envelope reads the 3 kVA rule against each home's own annual peak, which is debatable.

Bruce: Dating each charger's arrival from the meters is a creative Part 1 gain plus a managed-charging rung, though the NET row still rests on assumed prices and the result depends on how the 3 kVA rule is read.

Andrew: It measures the one rung every ladder assumes (a managed-charging envelope pass rate) and dates each charger's first Level 2 day for a measured adoption rate, so unlisted chargers become outreach triggers I could run, though it loosely ties the $73M to $106M capex to EV homes.

Mike: Change-point dating of new Level 2 chargers gives a meter-measured monthly EV adoption rate, which is forecasting gold, and it pairs that with a managed-charging pass rate that tests the cheap alternative to batteries, covering all three parts.

Brian: Dating each Level 2 charger's first day from the meter is a genuinely new use of the data and gives a measured adoption rate, but the managed-charging pass rate depends on an hourly-envelope reading of the 3 kVA rule that a reliability engineer may reject.

Rogerio: Dating charger onset from the meters gives a measured adoption rate and a real outreach trigger, but the managed-charging envelope relies on an hourly reading of the 3 kVA rule I would not accept as engineering approval.

Enrique: It ties all three parts into one story: change-point dating of new L2 chargers gives a meter-measured adoption rate, and a managed-charging rung tests the battery ladder; the risk is that the 3 kVA rule might be read as a nameplate limit.

Claudia: Meter-dated charger onset plus a managed-charging rung adds real Part 1 depth and a cheaper Part 3 route, but the pass rate hinges on an hourly-envelope reading of the 3 kVA rule, and it calls the pipeline's two-battery default 'the brief's default'.

Maureen: Dating charger onset from the meters is a fresh adoption-rate insight and the managed envelope fills the missing rung, but it narrows the story to EVs and its pass rate could land at 0% or 100% and lose contrast.
blockers: The proposal's envelope rule is a tautology: a home's own peak + 3 kW minus any hour's load is always at least 3 kW, so a throttled charger always delivers about 30+ kWh a night and the managed pass rate comes out 100%. The credible version must use the strict no-new-peak reading (61-89% measured) and state the interpretation on the slide.
The 3 kVA rule's meaning is untestable here. If a Reliability judge reads it as a nameplate limit, throttling counts only with a load-management device (EVEMS) assumed, and the deck has to say so.
Hourly data hides 15-minute peaks (README limitation), so every envelope pass rate is optimistic. Present it as screening for who gets studied, not as engineering approval.

No ground truth for onset dates: the EV list carries no install dates, so 'new during the year' cannot be validated, only bounded. Seasonal HVAC contaminates all-day detection (measured May-June false spike).
No geography in the data: the 'zip' in this repo means archive files, not postal ZIPs, so the ZIP-level charger count cannot be built. The proposal already cuts it first.
No managed-charging program cost or EV TOU tariff: the NET row runs on assumption.* prices and the checker will force them to be labeled.
No transformer or feeder map, so 'where unreported load is growing' stays at system level.
table.fallback: Drop onset dating and the ZIP map entirely. Ship the four-rung enablement ladder (none 0.7% / managed strict 61-89% across 10-25 kWh needs / one unit 56.6% / two units 100%), the per-customer routing CSV and the assumption-labeled NET row against the $73.4M-$106.1M battery path, with hidden chargers carried by the existing 392-unlisted and 51.4% facts. Build time about 6 h, all in analysis/bess.py plus checks. Judged against the rubric this keeps the parts the 40% Business Value block pays for: the battery prioritization method, quantified electrification enablement and an actionable routing table. It gives up the onset chart, which only added Innovation (10%) and an untestable Analytics claim.

reasons: Scott: Per-home PRISM change-point fits are classic, auditable load research and replace the flat 3.29 kW figure, but using the cooling slope to infer the heating load of a gas home is a shaky step, and the batteries matter little because 96.8% of homes already pass.

Bruce: Per-home change-point physics is excellent AMI-plus-weather work, but using a gas home's cooling slope to stand in for its heating load is an unvalidated leap that limits the battery and 3 kVA conclusions.

Andrew: A PRISM model for every home, with a cross-validated transfer from cooling to heating, is the most creative use of weather here and splits the 3,573 emerging homes for targeting, though the transfer can only be validated on a likely biased holdout.

Mike: Per-home PRISM change-point fits replace the flat 3.29 kW that the whole winter-flip claim rests on, with auditable per-home parameters and holdout validation, which is exactly what a forecaster can use; the cooling-to-heating transfer remains the weak inference.

Brian: A vectorized per-home PRISM change-point fit is auditable line by line, uses AMI and weather together better than anything else here, and replaces a flat 3.29 kW with per-home, cross-validated estimates, held back only by the unproven cooling-to-heating transfer.

Rogerio: Replaces the flat 3.29 kW with an engineer-checkable per-home design-day kW and 3 kVA verdict, cross-validated on 2,873 electric-heat homes, which is exactly the per-service evidence reliability needs.

Enrique: Per-home PRISM change-point models replace the flat 3.29 kW with an auditable, weather-driven, cross-validated figure for each home, which ties all three parts together and scales by vectorization; the cooling-to-heating transfer is the stated, testable risk.

Claudia: Per-home change-point thermal models are a credible upgrade on the flat 3.29 kW, but using the cooling slope as a proxy for gas-home heating load is unvalidated outside electric-heat homes, and it promises a date range with no adoption data.

Maureen: Per-home change-point thermal models are an elegant use of AMI and weather, but using cooling slope to stand in for gas-home heating load is an untested inference and the promised date range has no adoption data behind it.
blockers: Hard blocker on the core claim, measured today on the repo's own data: summer behaviour does not predict winter heating load in electric-heat homes (cooling-slope CV R2 about 0, all summer features 0.05). So the pipeline cannot rank gas-heated homes by predicted heat-pump kW, and 'recruit the lowest-kW homes first' cannot be supported. The proposal's own biggest-risk paragraph is confirmed, not hypothetical.

No data on gas-heated homes' thermal size: no gas usage, floor area, building age or insulation. 6,755 active homes have neither electric heat nor AC, so they have no cooling slope to transfer from at all.

Resistance vs heat-pump confusion: class.heat_pump confidence is 'low' and labeled-HP recall is 16.7%, so the training set mixes COP 1 and COP 2-3 homes and the COP curve's anchor (0.051 kW/F) is a blend.
Selection bias the proposal names: electric-heat homes differ from gas homes, and no data exists to test the transfer on gas homes.
Low decision stakes for the per-home 3 kVA list: 96.8% already pass with no battery under the current rule, and only 672 homes are enabled by a battery.
No adoption-rate data: a 'date range' for the winter flip needs an assumed conversion pace, which must be recorded as assumption.* and labeled on the slide.

No transformer or feeder map: the flip point stays system-level (sum of 25,653 homes), so it cannot say which feeder flips first. Hourly data also hides 15-minute peaks, which makes the 3 kVA test optimistic.
Single design hour: the 2.1F winter peak (2026-02-08 17:00) is one hour of one winter, so the design-day kW rests on a thin tail.
table.fallback: Ship the 'range, not ranking' version in about 8 h, reusing segment.py's flip block, bess.passes() and facts.record(). Replace the flat 3.29 kW with the measured spread of added winter-peak kW across the 2,873 electric-heat homes, which runs from 1.8 to 5.8 kW (10th to 90th percentile), with half above 3 kW. Bootstrap it into the 5,100-home flip point with a 90% interval. Report the per-home share of conversions expected to fail 3 kVA as a probability, not a list. Show the failed transfer test (CV R2 about 0) openly as the reason per-home targeting needs one more data source, such as gas billing or building records, and name that as the next step for Customer Programs. Rubric fit: this helps Impact Quantification and Actionability for Load Forecasting and Reliability (40% block), and Transparency and Rigor through an honest holdout (35% block), plus the 'improves planning and electrification' bonus. It adds nothing to classification accuracy or BESS prioritization, and it loses the per-home targeting story the proposal leads with. That is why it scores 2, not 3: the hours fit (about 17 for the full build) but the headline decision it promises cannot be supported.

reasons: Scott: It replaces perfect-foresight MW with P90 firm MW by season from a dispatch with state-of-charge limits, back-to-back event days and no foresight. That is the deliverable-capacity number load research and storage can actually stand behind.
Bruce: It replaces the perfect-foresight 14.86 MW with P90 firm MW from state-of-charge, day-ahead-triggered dispatch, which is the number a storage program actually files and accredits.

Andrew: It replaces the perfect-foresight 14.86 MW with a P90 firm MW figure from a day-ahead dispatch that tracks state of charge across back-to-back events, which is the number a VPP program can actually commit, and it combines technical rigor with business value.

Mike: It fixes the perfect-foresight flaw in the 14.86 MW figure with a day-ahead trigger, state-of-charge limits and a P90 firm MW, the most credible capacity number on offer, though the merit order still depends on an unvalidated thermostat shed.

Brian: Dispatch without perfect foresight, tracking state of charge across back-to-back event days, honestly corrects the overstated 14.86 MW to a P90 firm figure, which is real battery rigor, but the merit order still rides on assumed prices and an unvalidated 33% shed.

Rogerio: P90 firm MW from a no-foresight, state-of-charge-limited dispatch over back-to-back event days is the capacity number a reliability director can actually trust, replacing the perfect-foresight 14.86 MW.

Enrique: Replacing the perfect-foresight 14.86 MW with a state-of-charge, day-ahead-triggered P90 firm-MW dispatch is the most operationally honest battery assessment in the set, though it is dense to present.

Claudia: Swapping a perfect-foresight 14.86 MW for P90 firm MW, with day-ahead weather triggers and state-of-charge limits, gives the auditable, deliverable capacity number a regulator can credit, though every dollar on the merit order is still a placeholder.

Maureen: Replacing the perfect-foresight 14.86 MW with a P90 firm MW from state-of-charge dispatch is the most operationally honest battery number, though 'firm kW-yr' needs more explaining than a general audience gets.
blockers: Soft blocker: there are no program costs for thermostat DR, pool timers or managed charging, and no capacity value. Every $ per firm kW-yr is an assumption.* placeholder, so the merit order and its knee, which carry the proposal's 'thermostats first, fewer batteries' decision, rest on assumptions and can flip. Battery cost has a cited anchor (GMP lease). Flex program costs have none in sources/.

Untestable assumption: thermostat shed % cannot be validated without real DR event data. The SCE 0.73 kW per home figure is a sanity anchor, not a validation, and the summer ranking flips between 20% and 33% shed.
No transformer or feeder map, so firm MW is system-level only. There is no locational value and no local constraint, and judges from reliability and storage policy will notice.
The 'forecast' is built from the same weather file (no archived day-ahead forecasts), so forecast error is simulated, not observed.
Pool and EV L2 flex depend on Part 1 labels that are positive-only and unverified (EV list is a ~25% sample), so flex MW for those resources carries classification error.

Rubric risk, not a data blocker: this adds nothing to classification or segmentation (much of the 35% analytics weight), and judges may read it as repackaging Part 3. Its value is the operational-realism and impact-quantification lines (40%) and the 'innovative BTM BESS prioritization framework' bonus line.
table.fallback: Ship the firm-MW stack and drop the $ curve. analysis/vpp.py reports P50/P90 firm MW per season for batteries (day-ahead trigger, fixed window, no perfect foresight), set against the 14.86 / 11.32 MW paper figures. It adds thermostat (20/33/50% band, SCE-anchored) and pool-pump MW layered without double counting. It takes about 10-11 h, needs no missing data, and every number traces through make check. The merit order becomes one ranked table: MW per 1,000 enrolled homes by resource and season. Per-kW cost appears only as one flagged-assumption sensitivity line. If time is still short, keep only battery firm vs paper MW plus the thermostat band (about 6 h). That still answers the rubric's 'aligned with utility operational realities' and 'impact quantification' lines.

reasons: Scott: This is the most complete ladder: EV and heat-pump branches, a managed rung capped at 3 kW and checked against delivered kWh, and per-home break-even arithmetic that checks out ($11.6k of value against $18k to $26k), all inside a Part 1 to 2 to 3 story.
Bruce: A per-home cheapest-fix ladder with a computed $6.4k to $14.4k break-even, all from facts already in hand, turns the failing battery payback into a defensible non-wires test.

Andrew: This is the most complete ladder: an hour-by-hour 3 kVA replay for EVs and heat pumps, a per-home break-even and a supply curve per rung, so the existing finding that batteries enable electrification becomes a routing tool I could hand to my team.

Mike: The strongest of the ladder variants: an hour-by-hour managed-charging test that checks daily kWh, an explicit break-even, and a winter-flip overlay, though the avoided-upgrade value is still unsourced.

Brian: A clean, honest break-even reframing of the battery case with a kWh-delivery check on managed charging, but it is a hand-ordered ladder over the existing headroom test with no new modeling, and the avoided-upgrade value is still unsourced.

Rogerio: The most complete ladder: an hour-by-hour 3 kVA test, a capped-charger energy check, a per-home break-even of about $6.4k to $14.4k and a six-input sensitivity, carried by a clean Part 1 to 3 story.

Enrique: A competent least-cost ladder with a per-home break-even column, but its thermostat and pool DR first rung does not belong in a service-headroom test, and the 3-million scale claim is asserted, not shown.
Claudia: A complete ladder that checks managed charging still delivers a median EV's kWh and reports a per-home break-even, which is solid, but its value still stops at a threshold no source fills.
Maureen: It carries the whole Part 1 to 2 to ladder story with a traced break-even and a winter-flip overlay, held back only by a DR rung that does not belong in a service-capacity test.
blockers: No service-upgrade cost in the data or the cited sources. The battery-vs-study decision can only be shown as a break-even dollar figure that judges must accept as plausible. This is a soft blocker, worked around by framing.

Ladder degeneracy. With the rule coded as new peak <= old peak + 3 kW, managed overnight charging at 3 kW or less passes about 100% of homes by construction. The battery steps would then hold about 0 homes unless the ladder is conditioned on a customer who declines managed charging or needs full 7.2 kW evening charging. That weakens the headline 'batteries only where they replace an upgrade' (rubric: Quality of Recommendations).

All $ inputs are assumptions (unit cost, TOU spread, capacity value $/kW-yr, 33% thermostat shed), so payback and break-even are illustrative until replaced with NYSEG/RG&E tariffs and avoided-cost values.
The 3 kVA test runs on hourly averages and understates 15-minute peaks, so pass rates are optimistic. Reliability and Regulatory judges are likely to raise this.
No transformer/feeder map, so 'coincident MW' is system-level and the per-home headroom ignores shared-transformer limits (the 392 unlisted L2 chargers cannot be placed on a transformer).
The winter-flip overlay cannot be tested: 5,100 is an aggregate, and no fuel/gas data says which homes would convert.
The 9.9 MW thermostat figure rests on an assumed 33% shed with no M&V data, and it is a summer figure while EV binding hours are winter/evening.
table.fallback: Ship an EV-only ladder with four steps: managed charging, one IQ 10C, two IQ 10C, service study. It reuses passes() per home and adds outputs/ladder.csv, a funnel of homes and MW per step from the existing ev_pass_pct_* results (0.7% none, 56.6% one unit, 100% two units), and one [NET] slide that puts the break-even avoided-upgrade cost at the low and high unit cost beside the 23 to 33 year peak-only payback, with every $ labeled as an assumption. The managed-charging step is presented as conditional ('if the customer accepts a 3 kW overnight cap'), and the battery steps cover customers who decline it. Cut the HP branch, the sensitivity table and the winter-flip overlay, in that order. This is about 6 to 7 build hours and still answers the rubric's battery methodology and electrification enablement items.

reasons: Scott: A bottom-up 8,760-hour scenario engine with a check that the zero-adoption run reproduces 59.4 and 42.6 MW gives forecasting a crossover band it can defend, and it re-ranks batteries by season. It only gives a threshold, never a year.
Bruce: A strong planning insight with an honest threshold band and a zero-adoption self-check, but battery re-ranking for a winter peak that does not yet bind is only a conditional recommendation.
Andrew: A clean adoption-to-peak curve and a real T1/T3 seasonal swap make a strong story, but without an adoption-rate input it risks reading as the existing 5,100-home number redrawn.

Mike: A bottom-up hourly scenario engine whose zero-adoption run must reproduce 59.4 and 42.6 MW, swept with bands and tied to re-ranking batteries for whichever season binds: forecasting and BESS value in one curve, though the per-home increment is still flat.

Brian: A bottom-up scenario engine whose zero-adoption run must reproduce 59.4 and 42.6 MW exactly is what an engineer trusts, and it turns the winter flip into a band plus a winter-weighted battery reorder, though without an adoption forecast it can give only a threshold.

Rogerio: A bottom-up 8,760 scenario engine that must reproduce 59.4 and 42.6 MW at zero adoption, with a crossover band and a season-aware battery re-rank, is planning-grade and honest about not printing a year.

Enrique: Bottom-up hourly re-summation gives a credible adoption-to-peak curve and reorders batteries toward the T1 winter tier, but it can give only a threshold, not a date, and the per-conversion kW leans on the weak heat-pump split.

Claudia: A bottom-up engine that must reproduce 59.4 and 42.6 MW at zero adoption, with a crossover band and MW per lever, is auditable planning evidence, but it can only give a threshold, not a year, and risks restating the existing 5,100-home number.

The lists are not random samples of owners: 51.4% of listed EVs show no home Level 2 charging, and 48.3% of listed HPs show under 1,500 kWh of heating (mini-splits). The verification sample has no survey or site-visit cost, so 'verify N homes' cannot be priced into a budget. Its interval-narrowing figure is model-simulated, and nothing in the data can check it.

The comparison is close to tautological: a ~$100-300 thermostat program beats an $18k-26k two-unit battery per kW under any plausible price, so an Energy Storage policy judge may read the result as built into the inputs. No winter thermostat lever exists today (flex.* is summer AC only), and the electric-heat shed share would be another unvalidated assumption.
No transformer or feeder map: MW is system-coincident, while real DR/BESS filings are often locational. No tariffs or avoided-cost values: CAP_VALUE $100/kW-yr is a placeholder.

Per-home thermostat kW is 33% of event load above the mild-day baseline on positive-unlabeled AC flags. Hourly data hides 15-minute peaks, so the 3 kVA result is optimistic. 10,072 of 35,725 customers are missing.

Brian: A who-pays ledger is a fresh lens, but with no income data it is bill exposure inferred from load shape, sits at the edge of the challenge, and its TOU results swing on tariffs that still have to be sourced.

reasons: Scott: The data-quality gate and the monthly change feed show real operational maturity and scalability, but the work is mostly plumbing on one replayed year, so it adds little business value or MW.
Bruce: Excellent scalability and data-quality plumbing, but it adds almost nothing to the battery value case, which carries most of the 40% business-value weight.
Andrew: Excellent scalability and data-quality story, but a one-year replay of plumbing adds almost nothing to the 40% business value and gives me no new program decision.

Mike: The data-quality gate and monthly feed are real operational value and maximize scalability, but they are plumbing that scores poorly on the deck's 40% business value, and with one year of data the change detection is only a replay.

Brian: A data-quality contract that would have caught the dropped zip, plus a measured scaling benchmark, is excellent engineering, but it is plumbing that adds almost nothing to the 40% business-value weight, and one year of data makes the monthly change feed a replay.
Rogerio: Operationally the most deployable (data-quality gate that catches the duplicated zip, measured scaling), but it is plumbing that earns little of the 40% business-value weight.
Enrique: Strong on scalability and data-quality contracts (it would have caught the duplicated zip), but it is plumbing that earns little of the 40% business-value weight on a deck-only score.
Claudia: The data-quality gate and measured scaling are strong engineering, but a monthly feed replayed on one year of data is plumbing that earns little of the 40% business-value weight.
Maureen: It scores top marks on scalability and catches the duplicated-zip defect, but it is plumbing on a one-year replay and does little for the 40% business-value weight.
blockers: Only one year of data (Sep 2025 to Aug 2026). Monthly change detection is a replay of one year, not live drift. Homes that had a charger all year show up in September, and a home that first shows Level 2 blocks later could be a new charger, a new EV or just seasonal driving. Without a later year or install dates, the 'new charger found' count cannot be tested.

The Level 2 rule needs weather-neutral days, and Nov to Feb have none. In those months the rule detects nothing unless a new winter rule is built, and that rule will mix up 6-7 kW EV blocks with resistance heat (soft blocker, and it eats about 3 of the 23 hours).

The electric-heat and heat-pump rules fit slopes across a whole heating season. Monthly flags from part of a season are noisy until about February, so the winter-flip counter can only show settling, not real month-to-month conversions.

The battery rank and 3 kVA status in the change feed depend on bess.py's top-10 seasonal event days and full-year shave. A monthly re-rank is not meaningful before both seasons are in, and no tariff or program cost exists to value an earlier offer.
The benefit side of the NET line ('value of one avoided transformer surprise') has no data behind it: no transformer or feeder map, no upgrade costs. It can only be an assumption.
The 3M-customer extrapolation is a curve fitted from runs at 10x or less on one laptop. 100x (about 90 GB) is not runnable here, and a cloud cost needs a cited price.

Rubric fit (soft): the deck is all the panel scores. This idea mainly hits Innovation/Scalability (one bullet in the 10% criterion) and Transparency & Reproducibility (part of the 35%). It adds almost nothing to the 40% Business Value criterion (battery assessment, impact quantification), so the hours compete with work that scores more.
Budget: about 23 h is nearly the whole 24 person-hour build budget for the team, leaving nothing for the Part 1-3 work the rubric weights most.

(2) Measured scaling at 1x, 2x and 4x customer shards, with time and memory per home and a straight-line extrapolation to 3M labeled as arithmetic: 3 h. (3) One replay chart of when each of the 564 Level 2 homes first shows charging, using the existing rule only in months with enough weather-neutral days (Sep and Apr-Aug), and saying plainly that this is a one-year replay with winter excluded: 3 h. (4) facts keys and make check: 1 h. Cut, in order: the cloud-cost line, monthly battery re-ranking, the winter Level 2 rule, the 10x benchmark, the electric-heat settling curve and the winter-flip counter. The NET line stays out unless its benefit is clearly labeled an assumption.

reasons: Scott: The records-versus-meters story is compelling, but the asset stress counts come from random synthetic transformer groups with assumed kVA ratings, which is speculation presented as analysis.
Bruce: The non-wires siting idea is right, but asset stress built on synthetic transformer groups with assumed kVA ratings and a 30.5% L2 precision floor reads as speculation.
Andrew: The headline asset-stress numbers would rest on synthetic transformer groupings and assumed kVA ratings, which reads as speculation to a utility panel.
Mike: Hidden load against recorded load is the right planning question, but asset stress rests on synthetic transformer groups and assumed kVA ratings, and it carries a 30.5% L2 precision floor.

Brian: Its asset-stress results come from random synthetic transformer groupings at assumed kVA ratings, with hidden loads carried at a 30.5% precision floor, so the overload claims are speculation dressed as analysis.
Rogerio: Records-vs-meters hidden load at peak is the reliability question I care most about, but every asset-overload number rests on synthetic transformer groups and a 30.5% L2 precision floor.
Enrique: Comparing hidden load with recorded load is a compelling planning frame, but the asset roll-up needs synthetic transformer groupings and leans on an L2 precision floor of only 30.5%.

Claudia: The hidden-load idea is compelling, but every asset-stress result comes from synthetic transformer groupings at assumed kVA ratings plus a 30.5% L2 precision floor, so it is speculation I could not put in a filing.
Maureen: Records versus meters is an intuitive reliability story, but the asset stress numbers rest on random synthetic transformer groups at assumed ratings and a 30.5% L2 precision floor.
blockers: Soft blocker, no transformer, feeder or any geography in the data. The proposal says the rollup 'today runs on zip', but no zip code exists (the zips are archive files). So every asset-level overload number rests on random synthetic groups and assumed kVA ratings. That is the headline decision (inspection and upgrade order), and the Director Reliability judge can dismiss it as speculation

The hidden L2 count cannot be tested. 392 = flags minus implied listed owners, which assumes every unlisted flag is a real charger. The 30.5% precision floor counts only listed owners as true, so per-home 'hidden EV' vs false positive (well pump, sauna, dryer, water heater) cannot be told apart. The register must show a band, not a point

'Heat mostly unlisted' is true by construction: no resistance-heat list was given, and the HP list is a 25% sample. Avangrid may already know electric-heat homes from a heating rate code, which would erase the 'hidden' half of the claim. This cannot be checked with the data we have

The rubric's Impact Quantification criterion has no dollar figure available: no upgrade costs or transformer replacement costs, and the battery value rests on assumption.* prices (23 to 33 year payback). 'Battery defers an upgrade' stays qualitative unless an assumed $/upgrade is added and labeled
The 3 kVA rule is written for added load needing a study. For load already installed, the test becomes a counterfactual (peak without the load + 3 kW). Service size (200 A) is assumed for every home
Heat-pump detection is low-confidence (AUC 0.718, held-out recall 16.7%), so any HP vs resistance split in the register is weak
Hourly data hides short peaks (the raw files note 4 x 15-min intervals but ship only hourly sums), so stress is understated

Scope risk: the requirements.yaml off_problem rule fails the deck on outage/SAIDI/SAIFI. An 'overload found when an asset fails' story slides toward the outage topic the judges told us is out of scope
table.fallback: Ship the per-meter register only (about 10 h): hidden_loads.csv ranked by probability-weighted kW at the summer and winter event hours, with a low/high band (precision floor to upper bound). Add a system-level total of unrecorded MW at the coincident peaks, as a share of insight.system_peak_mw and insight.winter_peak_mw. Tag each home with its cheapest fix through the reused passes() (managed charging, 1 or 2 IQ 10C, field check), which feeds the rubric's Battery Opportunity and electrification-enablement criteria. Drop the synthetic transformer overload counts from the main deck. Keep at most one clearly labeled sensitivity in the appendix. Make the meter-to-transformer CSV schema the single ask of Avangrid ('run this file and the asset table fills in'), which serves Scalability and Actionability without claiming asset results the data cannot support.
